The required licensure test for Secondary Physics (license code 320) is Praxis test 5266 with a required score of 145.
Permit to Teach: the applicant must hold at least a bachelor's degree and never have been issued any other NC professional educator license. The school unit's governing body requests it.
A Permit to Teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

For State Salary Schedule pay, a Permit to Teach is issued at the bachelor's (A-Level) zero-experience level regardless of education or prior work experience, so the applicant's 4 years of industry work would not raise pay on this license.

Emergency License: the applicant must hold a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours of coursework relevant to the area, must not have completed a recognized EPP in that area, and must not qualify for a Residency License. The school unit requests it.
An Emergency License is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.
For salary, an Emergency License is issued at the A-Level, but the holder may qualify for graduate degree pay or experience pay under LICN-006.

Residency License: the applicant must meet G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and have either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure exam. The school unit requests it.

Renewal of a Residency License requires enrollment in a recognized EPP, employment as a teacher, at least six months of teaching in the preceding school year, and 10 days of professional development in the first year.

Because the Emergency License is available only if the applicant does not qualify for a Residency License, an applicant who passes Praxis 5266 or completes 24 physics-relevant hours would qualify for the Residency License instead. An applicant with 18 to 23 relevant hours who has not passed the exam would fall under the Emergency License.

Experience credit for non-teaching work: full-time relevant work completed after the bachelor's degree earns one year of credit for every year, but only if it is at least 20 hours per week, was completed after age 18, was not on-the-job training, was paid and documented, and the school unit recommends it. Under this rule, 4 full years would be up to 4 years of salary credit.

Non-teaching experience must be directly related to the licensure area. DPI considers alignment with the Standard Course of Study content, transferable skills, and specialized knowledge beyond traditional EPP training.

A continuing professional teacher license requires holding an initial professional or residency license in NC, passing the licensure exam before or during the third year, at least three years of licensed teaching, and a Beginning Teacher Support Program (unless exempt). The passages list only the IPL or Residency License as starting points.

An Initial Professional License generally requires completing an EPP (in NC or outside NC) or holding an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of teaching. An applicant with only an engineering degree and industry experience would not meet these routes unless they hold an out-of-state clear license.
Any NC license application requires disclosure of any criminal history and prior license suspensions or revocations, and proof of any out-of-state license if held.

question: Candidate has a PhD in curriculum and instruction, no K-12 classroom time, wants to be an admin. Eligible?

answer.summary: The passages do not give a yes or no yet. Eligibility turns on which administrator license the candidate seeks and whether the PhD came from a State Board-approved administrator preparation program (APP). claims.text: An administrator license requires the applicant to meet G.S. 115C-270.20(b)(1) and the other applicable requirements in LICN-011.
For any administrator license other than superintendent, the applicant must have completed an administrator preparation program at the master's (M), specialist (S), or doctoral (D) level.

An APP is a program approved by the State Board of Education to prepare, train, and recommend candidates for administrator licensure. A PhD in curriculum and instruction qualifies only if it was completed through such a program, and the passages do not say whether this one was.
For a principal license, the master's degree must be in School Administration, Educational Leadership, or another education-related field.

To qualify for a superintendent license, the applicant must complete an APP at the specialist or doctoral level. Alternatively, a person may serve as superintendent with a bachelor's or higher from a regionally accredited institution plus five years of leadership or managerial experience deemed relevant by the hiring local board. DPI must verify those credentials before employment, and that route does not itself entitle the person to a superintendent license.

An applicant is eligible only for the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP or APP. A PhD completed through an APP would therefore set the degree level, though graduate salary pay under LICN-006 may also apply.

Examination requirements apply. For the Curriculum-Instructional Specialist license, the required test is Praxis 5412 with a required score of 146. For principal, the requirement is completion of the North Carolina Principal Portfolio Assessment with a validated score.

question: Teacher's NC CPL expired 3 years ago, now wants to return to teaching at a different district. Options?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

input.query: Teacher's NC CPL expired 3 years ago, now wants to return to teaching at a different district. Options?
expired continuing professional license reinstatement or apply for initial professional license after expiration
license expired lapsed no longer valid apply new license requirements
licensure examination requirement applicant previously held license expired

answer.summary: The main option in the passages is a validation of the expired CPL, which the new district's governing body can request, but only if the teacher was not employed by any public school unit during the preceding fiscal year. Whether that condition is met, and the teacher's license area and CEU status, determine the path, so those facts are needed before advising.

claims.text: A PSU governing body may request that DPI validate an expired CPL issued to an applicant under its employment, even if the educator does not have the requisite CEUs, provided the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year.

A validated CPL is effective for three years, and the educator must complete the relevant renewal requirements in LICN-030, LICN-031, or LICN-032 by the end of the third year to renew the CPL for a new five-year renewal cycle.

A CPL is a five-year renewable license. Teachers holding a CPL must renew every five years, completing 8 CEUs per cycle: for Grades 6-12, 4 CEUs in the license area and 4 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment; for Pre-K through Grade 5, 3 license-area CEUs, 3 literacy CEUs, and 2 general CEUs.

Renewal of a CPL by a teacher employed by a local board also requires evidence of a rating of at least 'proficient' on the most recent annual evaluation in NCEES (three of five standards proficient, including Standard 4).

The fee for validating an expired CPL is listed as $60 in the fee schedule. That schedule is marked effective 2018-04-05 and its fees apply to applications opened effective January 1, 2017, so the current amount should be confirmed.
An application is complete only when all required information is submitted, the application fee is paid, and any required investigation clearance is obtained.

If the teacher does not qualify for validation, an Initial Professional License route is available for an applicant who has completed a recognized NC EPP and is recommended by it, who completed an out-of-state EPP, or who holds a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction. The passages do not say whether a former NC CPL holder qualifies under these routes.

A PSU governing body may request an IPL for an applicant under its employment who has completed all academic and field requirements for a recognized NC EPP but has not satisfied the licensure exam requirements, without the EPP recommendation.

questions_for_user: When was the teacher last employed by any North Carolina public school unit, and was that employment in the fiscal year immediately before the validation request? This determines whether validation under LICN-033 §3 is available.
What license area and grade band is the teacher's CPL in? This determines the CEU requirements and whether any renewal path applies.
How many CEUs does the teacher have, and was the most recent annual evaluation rated proficient?
Has the teacher held any other NC license, or any out-of-state license? Which EPP did the teacher complete, and in what year?
Is the new district requesting validation now, and has the teacher completed the required licensure exams?

Whether a validated CPL can be transferred between districts, or how the new district's employment affects it.
The conversion of CEUs to hours, and how CEUs earned before expiration are counted.
Fees and processing timelines for the current fiscal year, since the fee schedule provided is dated 2018.
The effect of the April 15 application deadline (LICN-001 §3(f)) on this request; the passages do not say whether it applies to validation.

However, the answer omits the mandatory improvement plan IPL path, the LICN-007 §8 point that reinstatement does not govern an expired CPL, the June 30 expiration rule, and the April 15 timing consideration.

claims.text: An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license for an applicant or professional educator who meets the relevant SBE requirements.

To qualify for a continuing professional teacher license, an applicant must hold an IPL or residency license in North Carolina, satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements, have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

With 2 years of licensed teaching experience, the teacher falls short of the three-year minimum by 1 year (3 required minus 2 held = 1 year remaining), so the CPL requirement in LICN-024 §1(c) is not met today.

The art license's required examination is Praxis 5135 with a required score of 161; the policy requires the examination to be satisfied before or during the third year of licensure, and an applicant who did not satisfy it before receiving the IPL must attempt it at least once during the first year.

An exception to the Beginning Teacher Support Program requirement applies if the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina, or previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL under LICN-030.

The policies provided do not allow partial years to be combined to satisfy the licensed teaching experience requirement for a CPL; the partial-year combination rule appears only in the salary experience credit policy, which is not a licensure rule.

question: Teacher is on an RL in special ed, 2 years in, wants to add a general ed K-12 area. Can they do both on one RL?

input.query: Teacher is on an RL in special ed, 2 years in, wants to add a general ed K-12 area. Can they do both on one RL?
Residency License add additional license area or add-on teaching area
definition of clear license residency license not a clear license

answer.summary: On the passages, the teacher cannot add the general education area to the existing residency license, because LICN-013 bars adding teaching areas to a residency license. A separate residency license in the new area may be possible under LICN-019 §4, but only if the teacher holds a clear license in another area, and the passages do not say whether a residency license counts as clear. Confirm the teacher's license holdings and the exact K-12 area before deciding.

claims.text: DPI shall not add additional teaching license areas under LICN-013 §1 to a residency license, so a teacher holding a residency license cannot have a new area added to that same license through the add-on process.

A governing body may request a residency license in an additional license area for an applicant under its employment only if the applicant holds a clear license in another area and meets the G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) requirements for each requested area. This describes a separate residency license request, not an addition to the existing one.

A clear license is a professional educator license that is in good standing, requires no additional professional examinations or coursework, has no revocation, discipline, or pending unprofessional-conduct investigation, and has not been surrendered under investigation. The passages do not state whether a residency license meets this definition. A residency license requires enrollment in a recognized EPP, which may be relevant to the 'no additional coursework' element, but the passages do not decide the question.

Under LICN-013 §2(b), Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can be added only by satisfying the licensure examination requirements, not by coursework alone. This applies to adding that area to an existing IPL or CPL, so it bears on any add-on route involving special education.

Adding a teaching area through coursework requires 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area with a grade of C or better in each course. This is the alternative to examination for areas that allow it, and it applies only to licenses eligible for add-on under LICN-013 §1.

The residency license must be renewed each year. Renewal requires enrollment in a recognized EPP, employment as a teacher, at least six months of teaching experience in the preceding school year, and, in the first year, 10 days of professional development. If the applicant does not satisfy the conversion requirements by June 30 of the third year, the residency license expires.

Teacher license classifications include Exceptional Children (Kindergarten through Grade 12) and Special Subjects (Kindergarten through Grade 12). General education K-12 is not a single classification in the passages, so the requested area must be matched to a specific classification such as Elementary (K-6), Middle Grades (6-9), Secondary (9-12), or Special Subjects (K-12).

questions_for_user: Does the teacher hold any clear license (an IPL or CPL, not a residency license) in any area? LICN-019 §4 requires one for a separate residency license in a new area.
Is the special education residency license in an Exceptional Children classification, and which one?
Which specific general education area is requested (Elementary K-6, Middle Grades, Secondary 9-12, or a Special Subjects area)? 'K-12' does not match a single teacher classification in the passages.
Is the teacher asking to add the area to the existing residency license or to have a second residency license issued? The answer differs under LICN-013 §3(c) and LICN-019 §4.
Has the teacher already completed the first-year 10 days of professional development, and is the current renewal documentation in order?
premise_corrections: The passages do not allow adding a general education area to the existing residency license. LICN-013 §3(c) prohibits adding teaching areas to a residency license. The only route in the passages is a separate residency license under LICN-019 §4, which requires a clear license in another area.
not_covered: Whether a residency license qualifies as a 'clear license' under LICN-001 §2(f).
The requirements of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which LICN-019 §4 incorporates by reference.
Whether the teacher's general education K-12 request maps to a specific classification and what that classification requires.
Whether the teacher would qualify for a separate residency license in the new area under LICN-019 §1(a), which requires 24 hours of coursework or passing the licensure exam in that content area.
Any rules on the timing of a second residency license relative to the first one's three-year window.
Whether the first-year 10 days of professional development requirement in LICN-019 §2(a)(iv) was met, since the passages do not show records of completion.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly states that the add-on rules bar adding the general education area to the residency license and identifies the separate residency license route and the clear-license question. It omits the conversion-to-IPL/CPL route by June 30 of year three, which is a key path to the goal, and does not note that one renewal remains. claims.text: A teacher license generally requires completion of an educator preparation program at the Bachelor's (A), Master's (M), Specialist (S), or Doctoral (D) level. An associate's degree (V-Level) is not on that list.

An applicant with only a high school diploma or an associate's degree may be issued a teacher license only in Career and Technical Education, Junior Reserve Officer Training Corps, or Safety and Driver Education. Early childhood/pre-K is not among these areas.

An applicant is eligible for a license only at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP.

An Emergency License requires at least a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours of relevant coursework, no completed EPP in that licensure area, and not qualifying for a Residency License. It cannot be extended or renewed.

A Residency License may be requested by a PSU for an applicant who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either 24 hours of coursework in the content area or has passed the applicable licensure exam. The passages do not reproduce the statute's degree requirements.
A Limited License may be requested by a PSU for an applicant who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(4a). It may only be issued for teaching license areas. The statute's content is not in the passages.
A Pre-K license requirement for an associate-degree holder is not specified in the passages beyond the classifications above.

question: Applicant from Tennessee, 7 yrs teaching special ed, has a current TN license but it's in a different category than NC EC. Which NC license fits?

input.query: Applicant from Tennessee, 7 yrs teaching special ed, has a current TN license but it's in a different category than NC EC. Which NC license fits?

answer.summary: With 7 years of licensed teaching experience, the applicant falls under the out-of-state Continuing Professional License pathway in LICN-025 §2, not the Initial Professional License pathway. claims.text: An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license under LICN-025 §2. An applicant with fewer than three years qualifies for an IPL under LICN-025 §1(a) instead, so the 7 years of experience points to the CPL pathway.

Under LICN-025 §2, the applicant must meet both (a) holding a clear license from another jurisdiction and (b) either holding NBPTS certification or having licensure requirements substantially similar to NC's.

A clear license must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, not subject to a pending unprofessional conduct investigation, and not voluntarily surrendered during an investigation.

Substantially similar means the other jurisdiction required, at minimum, completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on an out-of-state exam, and the applicant must pass the applicable exam for each NC license area sought under LICN-010.
Exam results must be presented at the time of initial NC licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

Exceptional Children license areas in NC include Adapted Curriculum, General Curriculum, Learning Disabled, Cross Categorical, Severely/Profoundly Disabled, Mentally Disabled, Academically or Intellectually Gifted, Deaf and Hard of Hearing, Visually Impaired, and Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled.

The NC exam requirements for EC areas are listed by area and licensure code in LICN-003 §5. Each EC area has its own required tests and scores, so the applicant's exam results must be checked against the specific area sought.
A teacher license is issued in the license area(s) indicated on it, and an applicant is eligible only at the highest degree level at which they completed an EPP.

Adding an EC: General Curriculum area to an existing license can only be done by satisfying the exam requirements, not by coursework alone. Adding a teaching area after NC licensure under LICN-025 §4 follows LICN-013.
A CPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

The BTSP requirement for out-of-state applicants applied through LICN-025 (LICN-024 §1(d) addresses NC CPL applicants and mentions out-of-state experience but is not clearly tied to the LICN-025 path).
Fees for the application (LICN-008 lists out-of-state IPL fees, but no CPL fee for out-of-state applicants).
Any rules in effect before 2026-07-01 for out-of-state CPL applicants.

Its claim that General Curriculum can only be added by exam is not stated in the cited LICN-013 text, and it omits the 24-credit coursework option.

An out-of-state exam is one recognized by the licensing authority of a jurisdiction outside North Carolina and necessary to be issued a renewable license there. The passages do not say whether any UK exam meets this definition.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a CPL. They must hold a clear license from another jurisdiction, meaning it is in good standing, renewable, not revoked or disciplined, and has no pending unprofessional-conduct investigation or surrender under investigation.

For a CPL, the applicant must also hold NBPTS certification, or the other jurisdiction's requirements must be substantially similar to NC's. Substantially similar means the applicant completed an EPP recognized by the state where it is located and passed an out-of-state exam for each license area sought.
Out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial NC licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use those results to convert an IPL to a CPL.
An applicant who completed an EPP outside North Carolina may qualify for an IPL under the general rule, separate from the out-of-state rule, without needing a clear license.

The four years of ESL teaching in London count toward the CPL experience test only if they are licensed professional educator experience. The passages do not say whether unlicensed teaching counts, or how UK licensing rules apply.

A Permit to Teach is available only to someone who has never been issued any other NC professional educator license, and it cannot be renewed. Because this applicant has a master's degree, the Permit to Teach is not the relevant route.
Salary effects are separate from licensure. Graduate salary pay requires an accredited master's in a directly related area and assignment in that area for at least 50% of the school day.

Under the general rule, every license expires on June 30 of the year it is set to expire, unless it is renewed, extended, or converted to another type of license under SBE policy. For an emergency license, LICN-018 §3 bars extension or renewal, so the June 30 expiration applies.
A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for an emergency license in the same license area.

An emergency license is eligible only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree with at least 18 relevant credit hours, has not completed a recognized educator preparation program in that licensure area, and does not qualify for a residency license.

For state salary schedule purposes, an emergency license is issued at the A-Level (bachelor's degree) teacher license level, but the holder may qualify for graduate degree pay or experience pay under LICN-006. LICN-006 is not among the passages provided, so those pay provisions cannot be described here.

question: Teacher has an RL in French and resigned mid-year, now at a private school. Does the RL clock stop?

input.query: Teacher has an RL in French and resigned mid-year, now at a private school. Does the RL clock stop?
residency license term clock stops when teacher leaves employment or resigns

license validity period clock paused break in employment expiration renewal not employed

answer.summary: The passages contain no provision that pauses or stops a residency license clock when a teacher resigns mid-year. The clock keeps running toward the June 30 deadline in the third year, and renewal depends on employment at a public school unit or an eligible nonpublic school. Confirm the teacher's license year, renewal history, and whether the private school is an eligible nonpublic school before advising.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.

To renew a residency license, the employing PSU governing body or eligible nonpublic school must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program, is employed as a teacher in the public school unit or eligible nonpublic school, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year of the license.

If an applicant fails to renew a residency license for the second or third year, the license expires. A PSU or eligible nonpublic school that hires the applicant within three years of the initial residency license's effective date may request reinstatement, provided the license has not already been renewed twice and the applicant is employed by that school and enrolled in an EPP.

To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL or CPL requirements and be recommended by the EPP. If the requirements are met by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL is effective when the requirements are met.

The only provision in the passages that suspends the residency license three-year timeframe is for active-duty servicemembers or their spouses who are called to duty or relocated outside North Carolina under military orders. The timeframe is held in abeyance until the servicemember returns to North Carolina and returns to employment in a North Carolina public school.

An eligible nonpublic school is defined by reference to G.S. 115C-207.20(a)(5)a.2, which is not included in the passages. Whether the teacher's new private school qualifies cannot be determined from the passages.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license (IPL) by either holding a license in the corresponding license area outside NC or having completed an educator preparation program recognized by the jurisdiction where that EPP is based.

Exam results for an IPL or CPL based on an out-of-state exam must be presented at initial NC licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

question: out of state cert in special ed mild/moderate, 0 yrs teaching, want nc EC. possible?

answer.summary: Likely yes: with fewer than three years of experience, this applicant can qualify for an NC Initial Professional License (IPL) in Cross Categorical (Mildly/Moderately Disabled), if they either hold a corresponding out-of-state license or completed a recognized EPP. The exam path then depends on whether they passed that state's exam, and otherwise on attempting and passing the NC Cross Categorical exams (5355 and 5511) on the timeline in LICN-025.

claims.text: An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license (IPL). The applicant with 0 years of teaching experience falls within this group.

To qualify for the IPL, the applicant must either hold a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction, or have completed an educator preparation program recognized by the jurisdiction where that EPP has its principal place of business.

Mild/moderate special education corresponds to the NC license area 'Exceptional Children: Cross Categorical (Mildly/Moderately Disabled)' in LICN-010 §6(e)(iv). This assumes the other state's license covers that same area; the passages do not map other states' license titles to NC areas.

Cross Categorical is not Elementary Education or Special Education: General Curriculum, so the third-year rule in LICN-025 §1(b) for those two areas does not apply. Instead, the applicant must either pass the out-of-state exam for that area (§1(b)(i)), or satisfy the NC examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, provided they attempted those exams at least once during the first year of licensure (§1(b)(ii)).
The NC examination requirements for Cross Categorical (licensure code 88001) are Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a required score of 145 and Test 5511 with a required score of 148.

If the applicant relies on an out-of-state exam pass, the exam results must be presented at the time of initial NC licensure, and those results cannot be used later to convert the IPL to a continuing professional license.
The IPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

Pre-2026 rules or what applied before the current effective dates; the passages cannot confirm this.

For any administrator license other than superintendent or Exceptional Children program administrator, the applicant must have completed an administrator preparation program at the Master's (M), Specialist (S), or Doctoral (D) level.
An administrator preparation program (APP) is a program approved by the State Board of Education to prepare and recommend candidates for administrator licensure.

A teacher with two courses remaining in an MSA has not yet completed an APP, so the completion requirement in LICN-011 §5 is not met as of now. The policies provided do not define when an APP is considered complete.
For a principal license, the master's degree must be in School Administration, Educational Leadership, or another education-related field.
The applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP or APP.

The applicant must satisfy any applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, provided the applicant attempts the examination at least once during the first year of licensure.

For principal, the examination requirement is the North Carolina Principal Portfolio Assessment with a validated score; for curriculum-instructional specialist, it is Praxis 5412 with a required score of 146.
An assistant principal in a PSU must hold either a principal license or a provisional assistant principal license issued under LICN-014, Section 7.

A CPL in English is a teacher license. Teacher license area does not determine administrator eligibility under the passages, and the teacher's five years of teaching experience is not an administrator-license requirement in the passages except through the superintendent-specific path in LICN-011 §3(b).

questions_for_user: Which administrator license is the teacher seeking (principal, curriculum-instructional specialist, assistant principal, or other)? Requirements differ by license type.
Is the MSA an approved administrator preparation program at the master's level, and is it in school administration, educational leadership, or a related education field?
What is the expected completion date for the two remaining courses?
Has the teacher already taken any required licensure examination (for example, Praxis 5412 or the Principal Portfolio Assessment)?
Is the teacher seeking an assistant principal role, which would require a provisional assistant principal license under LICN-014 Section 7 that is not in the provided passages?
premise_corrections: The question assumes eligibility to apply now. The passages require completed APP coursework, and the teacher has not yet completed the program.
not_covered: Whether an application may be submitted before the APP is completed, and how it would be processed (LICN-004 covers application contents but not timing for incomplete programs).
Requirements for the provisional assistant principal license under LICN-014 Section 7, which is not included in the passages.
The definition of when an APP is considered complete, and whether a partially completed program counts toward any requirement.
Statutory requirements under G.S. 115C-270.20(b)(1), which are referenced but not provided.
Whether the teacher's current CPL affects administrator licensure, beyond the passages' general statements.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key bottom line that the applicant cannot qualify until the M-level administrator preparation program is complete, and it covers the degree-field requirement, the teaching CPL not conferring eligibility, and the principal portfolio exam. It omits the SBE-approval dependence of the MSA, the IPL conditional, and the application documentation point, and its claims about the two remaining courses and the CPL go slightly beyond the cited text, but nothing it states is materially false.

question: Applicant has a Master of Arts in teaching from a NC IHE, passed all Praxis tests, no classroom experience, wants a Residency License in high school history. Eligible?

input.query: Applicant has a Master of Arts in teaching from a NC IHE, passed all Praxis tests, no classroom experience, wants a Residency License in high school history. Eligible?
educator preparation program completed initial professional license requirements
G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) residency license eligibility requirements

answer.summary: The applicant may be eligible for a Residency License in high school history if the Praxis 5581 score is at least 153 and the employing public school unit requests the license under LICN-019 §1(a). Passing the exam satisfies the alternative to 24 hours of coursework, but the applicant's actual score, the statute's (a)(5) requirements, and EPP recognition still need to be confirmed.

claims.text: A residency license may be requested by a public school unit governing body for an applicant under its employment if the applicant meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination requirements for that content area.
For Secondary (9-12) History (license code 420), the required ETS Praxis test is 5581 with a required score of 153.

The applicant's passing of all Praxis tests satisfies the examination alternative only if the 5581 score meets or exceeds 153, since the required score is the passing threshold for History. The applicant's actual score was not provided.

A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for a permit to teach or an emergency license in the same license area. This does not restrict a first residency license request.

A teacher license applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the Bachelor's (A), Master's (M), Specialist (S), or Doctoral (D) level, and is eligible for a license at the highest degree level completed at an EPP. A Master's degree from an EPP therefore supports an M-level license.

Any license requiring completion of an EPP requires that the EPP be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where the EPP has its principal place of business. Recognition of the applicant's NC IHE program for the history area should be confirmed.

The residency license renewal requires the employing unit to document enrollment in a recognized EPP, employment as a teacher, and at least six months of teaching experience in the preceding school year. The applicant's lack of classroom experience does not bar the initial request but would affect renewal.

The employing unit must provide at least three hours of field experience before the teacher begins classroom teaching and at least 10 hours over the first year, and 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license. The applicant's lack of experience makes these requirements particularly relevant.

questions_for_user: What is the applicant's score on the Praxis 5581 (Social Studies/History) exam, and does it meet the required 153?
Did the applicant pass the test required for History (5581), and was the applicant's test taken as the Praxis test for this license area?
Is the NC IHE Master of Arts in Teaching a recognized educator preparation program for secondary history?
Is the applicant currently employed by Union County Public Schools under its employment, so that the district can request the residency license?
Does the applicant hold any other license, or has the applicant previously held a residency or emergency license in history?
not_covered: The text of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which sets additional eligibility conditions for a residency license request, is not included in the passages.
Whether the applicant's NC IHE program is recognized by the SBE for the history area is not stated in the passages.
Whether the applicant's MAT degree qualifies as the content-area coursework is not addressed beyond the examination alternative.
The passages do not state what the applicant's specific test score must be beyond the 153 threshold, or how multiple test attempts are handled.

incorrect_statements: The answer treats EPP recognition of the applicant's NC IHE MAT as a condition still to be confirmed for residency eligibility, but LICN-019 does not require EPP completion for an initial residency license.
Claim 4 implies the applicant's Master's degree from an EPP bears on eligibility for this residency license, which the policies do not tie to initial residency eligibility.
The answer omits that the residency license is a one-year license renewable twice.
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly routes eligibility through PSU employment under LICN-019 §1(a), identifies Praxis 5581 at 153 as the history exam, and covers field experience and PD requirements. It wrongly suggests EPP recognition matters for initial eligibility and omits the one-year term and renewal limit.

question: Candidate earned a BS in health and PE from a Florida university and passed FL certification exams. Wants an NC PE license. Route?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

input.query: Candidate earned a BS in health and PE from a Florida university and passed FL certification exams. Wants an NC PE license. Route?
Physical Education license area requirements out-of-state exam passing score teacher license
out-of-state exam passing score examining jurisdiction license area Florida certification test equivalent

answer.summary: The likely route is an out-of-state Initial Professional License (IPL) based on his Florida EPP, which requires either a passing score on the Florida exam for the NC area or NC testing completed during the first year and passed by the third year. Confirm which Florida exams and scores he holds, whether he wants Physical Education or Health and Physical Education, and whether he has teaching experience, because those determine the path and whether he can later convert to a Continuing Professional License.

claims.text: A candidate with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an out-of-state IPL if he holds a license in the corresponding area in another jurisdiction, or completed an educator preparation program recognized by the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business.

For an IPL in a license area other than Elementary Education or Special Education: General Curriculum, the applicant must either achieve a passing score on an out-of-state exam for that license area in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the applicable NC examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, having attempted those exams at least once during the first year of licensure.

The NC required tests are Physical Education (license code 090) with test 5091 at a required score of 152, and Health and Physical Education (license code 095) with test 5857 at a required score of 160.

To use out-of-state exam results for an IPL or CPL, the applicant must present evidence of the exam results at the time of initial licensure in NC. An out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

An IPL may be converted to a clear Continuing Professional License only if the State Board required exam is taken at least once during the first year of the license and passed before or during the third year of the license.

A CPL based on an IPL requires at least three years of licensed teaching experience and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program, unless the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina or previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL.

The application must include official transcripts for the degree, EPP completion documentation, a disclosure statement covering any prior suspension or revocation and any criminal history, proof of any current out-of-state educator license, and documentation of licensure exam performance.

The fee schedule in the policy provided (effective 2018-04-05, based on applications opened January 1, 2017) lists $100 for an out-of-state Initial Professional License, compared with $70 for an in-state IPL.

questions_for_user: Which Florida exams did he pass, and what were the scores? Does either exam correspond to the NC test for the area he seeks (Physical Education 5091 at 152, or Health and Physical Education 5857 at 160)?
Does he want Physical Education (090) or Health and Physical Education (095)?
Does he hold a current, clear Florida teaching license in that area, and is it in good standing with no pending investigations or discipline?
How many years of licensed teaching experience does he have, in Florida or elsewhere? This determines IPL eligibility (under three years) and CPL timing and BTSP requirements.
Was the Florida EPP recognized by Florida as required under LICN-025 §1(a)(ii), and does he have official transcripts and EPP completion documentation?
Has he already been hired by a North Carolina public school unit, and does he have any prior suspension, revocation, or criminal history that must be disclosed?
not_covered: Whether the specific Florida exams he passed are the out-of-state exams accepted for the NC area under LICN-025 §1(b)(i), and what passing score Florida requires.
Whether Florida is recognized for EPP purposes under the LICN-025 §1(a)(ii) standard. The passages do not identify recognized jurisdictions or EPPs.
The content of the Beginning Teacher Support Program under TCED-016, which is referenced but not provided.
Whether the 2018 fee schedule in LICN-008 is still current.
Any rules applicable to the candidate before the current policy versions took effect. The provided policies cannot confirm what applied earlier.

incorrect_statements: Claim 4 states an IPL may be converted to a CPL 'only if' the exam is taken in year one and passed by year three, but the cited LICN-003 §3 says only that the license 'may be converted provided' these conditions are met, so 'only if' overstates the policy and omits the other CPL requirements such as clear license and experience.

The summary treats the candidate's Florida program as a recognized EPP on which the IPL route is based, although the policies do not establish Florida EPP recognition and the answer's own follow-up questions acknowledge this is unverified.
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line of needs_more_info with the IPL route, the out-of-state exam substitution, the NC test alternative with correct scores, and the fee, and it asks for the right facts. It overstates the CPL conversion condition as 'only if' and presumes the Florida EPP qualifies without verification.

question: Teacher holds a CPL in elementary education and an Emergency License in Spanish. Can they teach Spanish under the emergency license while holding the CPL?

input.query: Teacher holds a CPL in elementary education and an Emergency License in Spanish. Can they teach Spanish under the emergency license while holding the CPL?
holder of more than one license area concurrently teach under multiple licenses

answer.summary: The passages do not expressly address a teacher holding a CPL in one area and an emergency license in another, but they treat an emergency license as a valid teaching license in its licensure area until it expires on June 30 of the requested fiscal year. Confirm that the Spanish EL is still within its validity period and was requested by the employing unit for Spanish; if the teacher wants to keep teaching Spanish after it expires, the passages point to adding Spanish to the CPL under LICN-013.

claims.text: An emergency license (EL) is a one-year nonrenewable license issued to an individual who meets the requirements of LICN-018.
An emergency license is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

A governing body may request an EL for an applicant only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours of coursework relevant to the licensure area for which the applicant was hired, has not completed a recognized educator preparation program in that area, and does not qualify for a residency license.
Any person employed as a professional educator in a North Carolina public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license issued by DPI.
Emergency License and Continuing Professional License are both listed as teacher license classifications.
Spanish is a listed teacher license area at the secondary level (Grades 9-12) and as a special subject (Kindergarten-Grade 12).
A CPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

An applicant may add a new license area to an existing IPL or CPL by satisfying the licensure examination requirements for that area, or by completing 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in that area with a grade of C or better in each course.
DPI shall not add additional teaching license areas under LICN-013 §1 to an Emergency License.
Every license expires on June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire, unless renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

questions_for_user: What is the expiration date (fiscal year requested) on the Spanish emergency license?
Did the employing public school unit request the emergency license for Spanish, and was the teacher's bachelor's degree verified to include at least 18 credit hours of relevant Spanish coursework?
Has the teacher completed any Spanish coursework or an exam that could be used to add Spanish to the CPL?
Is the teacher's emergency license still active, or has it already expired?
not_covered: Whether a teacher may hold a CPL in one license area and an emergency license in another at the same time.
Whether holding a CPL in elementary education affects eligibility for, or the scope of, the Spanish emergency license.
Whether the emergency license authorizes teaching Spanish in any setting beyond the employing unit that requested it.
The policies cited for conversion of an emergency license to another license type, and any rules on what happens after it expires (not provided).
LICN-006 and other salary-schedule rules referenced in LICN-018 §4 (not provided).

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly says the policies do not expressly address concurrent holding and that the Spanish emergency license is valid for teaching Spanish only until June 30 of the requested fiscal year, with the add-on path as the durable route. It omits the Praxis 5195 score of 168, only partly conveys the residency bar, and its citations for the grade-level listing and the bar on adding areas to an emergency license show only fragments.

question: Candidate from Indiana with a Proficient license in English 9-12, 1 year teaching. Need NC RL or CPL?

input.query: Candidate from Indiana with a Proficient license in English 9-12, 1 year teaching. Need NC RL or CPL?

answer.summary: Based on the stated facts, the candidate cannot get an NC CPL yet because an out-of-state CPL requires more than three years of licensed experience and the candidate has one year. An IPL is the likely route from an out-of-state license, and a residency license may be possible if the candidate is employed by an NC public school unit and meets the 24-hour coursework or exam requirement, but the passages do not confirm the residency statute, so the analyst needs to confirm employment, coursework or exam status, and the Indiana license details.

claims.text: A CPL based on an out-of-state clear license requires more than three years of licensed professional educator experience. At one year, the candidate is about two years short of that threshold, so a CPL is not available on the stated facts.
A CPL based on possession of a clear license in another jurisdiction must meet the requirements of LICN-025.

A North Carolina CPL for a teacher also requires holding an IPL or residency license in North Carolina, at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an IPL by holding a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction, or by completing a recognized educator preparation program.
An applicant with a clear license from outside North Carolina and fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience qualifies for an IPL under LICN-020.

An out-of-state applicant for an IPL in English (not Elementary or Special Education) must either pass an out-of-state exam for English in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the NC exam requirements before or during the third year of licensure, having attempted the exam at least once in the first year.
For Secondary English (9-12), the NC required test is Praxis 5038 with a required score listed as 5038 - 167.

A residency license may be requested by the governing body of a public school unit for an applicant under its employment who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure exam for that content area.

The passages do not state whether an out-of-state applicant is eligible for a residency license, and the statute G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) that sets the residency criteria is not included in the passages.

A residency license converts to an IPL or CPL only if the applicant meets the LICN-020 IPL requirements or LICN-024 CPL requirements and is recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee, and conversion must occur by June 30 of the third year of the residency license.
The policies do not define a 'Proficient license.' The passages use 'Proficient' only as an evaluation rating, and refer to an out-of-state 'clear license' with specified criteria.

questions_for_user: Is the candidate employed by a North Carolina public school unit, which would be needed to request a residency license?
Does the candidate have at least 24 hours of coursework in English, or have they passed an English licensure exam (Indiana or Praxis 5038)?
What exactly is the Indiana 'Proficient' license? Is it a clear license in good standing, with no pending investigation or discipline?
Does the candidate's one year of teaching count as licensed teaching experience in Indiana?
Where did the candidate complete their educator preparation program, and did the EPP recommend them?
Does the candidate hold a National Board certification?
premise_corrections: The passages do not recognize a 'Proficient license' as a license type. The analyst should confirm the actual Indiana license title and whether it is a clear license under LICN-025 §2(a).
not_covered: G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which sets the residency license eligibility criteria.
Whether out-of-state applicants are eligible for a residency license.
TCED-016 Beginning Teacher Support Program requirements and exceptions.
Indiana license terms, validity, or what the Indiana 'Proficient' designation means.
Pre-2026-07-01 rules that may have applied to this candidate.

metrics.judge_rationale: The bottom line matches the key: no CPL at one year, IPL route, residency possible with employer request and 24-hour or exam condition, and more facts needed. It does not explicitly correct the draft's false premise that license level or years determine RL versus CPL, and it omits the IPL three-year nonrenewable term. All cited claims are backed by the quoted policy text.

question: Applicant with an online BA in liberal arts, 3 yrs as a para, wants a Permit to Teach in math. Possible?

input.query: Applicant with an online BA in liberal arts, 3 yrs as a para, wants a Permit to Teach in math. Possible?
permit to teach examination requirements bachelor's degree content area
online degree accreditation requirement for license eligibility

answer.summary: A Permit to Teach is possible only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license, and the employing school unit requests it. The three years as a para do not affect eligibility or pay level. Confirm the prior-license history first, since that fact decides the question.

claims.text: A governing body of a public school unit may request a permit to teach for an applicant under its employment only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license.
Because the permit requires that the applicant has never been issued any other NC professional educator license, a prior NC license of any type would make the applicant ineligible for a permit.

An online BA is a bachelor's degree on the face of the policy, so the degree element appears to be met if the applicant's degree is a bachelor's degree. The passages do not address whether online delivery or the awarding institution's accreditation affects permit eligibility.
A permit to teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

For State Salary Schedule pay, a permit to teach is set at the bachelor's (A-Level) zero-years-of-experience level regardless of the applicant's education level or prior work experience. The applicant's three years as a para therefore do not raise the pay level on a permit.

The permit policy sets no examination or coursework requirement specific to mathematics. The math licensure test table in LICN-003 is not stated to apply to permits, so the passages do not establish a math-specific requirement for this permit.
Math is a recognized license area for teachers (middle grades and secondary), but the passages do not say how a permit's license area is designated.
A permit to teach cannot have additional teaching license areas added to it.

questions_for_user: Has the applicant ever been issued any North Carolina professional educator license (including a permit, emergency, residency, or other license) or a lateral entry license? A prior license makes a permit ineligible.
Is the applicant's online BA a bachelor's degree conferred by an institution? Confirm the institution name and degree type.
Is the employing public school unit's governing body the one requesting the permit?
Does the applicant need the permit for a single school year (permits run to June 30 of the requested fiscal year)?
not_covered: Whether an online bachelor's degree or the awarding institution's accreditation affects permit eligibility.
Any examination or coursework requirement for a math permit specifically, beyond what LICN-017 states.
How a permit's math license area is designated or assigned.
Whether para or other non-teaching experience affects permit eligibility outside the salary pay level in LICN-017 §3.
What the applicant would need to move from a permit to a residency, emergency, or other license later.

incorrect_statements: A permit to teach cannot have additional teaching license areas added to it (cited LICN-013 §3(a) does not state this).
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's needs_more_info verdict and correctly identifies the degree, prior-license, PSU-request, salary-level, and validity rules. It hedges on whether accreditation or online delivery matters, where the key says the policy imposes no such requirement, and its final claim about adding license areas is unsupported by the cited text.

question: Teacher is on an RL in K-6, has taught 3 years, passed Praxis, took the required mentoring. Can they upgrade?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

input.query: Teacher is on an RL in K-6, has taught 3 years, passed Praxis, took the required mentoring. Can they upgrade?
residency license convert to continuing professional license requirements
fee for converting residency license to continuing professional license application
Beginning Teacher Support Program TCED-016 mentoring requirement

answer.summary: A residency license converts to an initial or continuing professional license only if the teacher meets the LICN-024 CPL requirements (or LICN-020 IPL requirements), has an EPP recommendation, and does so by June 30 of the third residency year. Before this can be confirmed, the analyst needs to verify the K-6 test scores (Praxis alone may not cover the required Pearson reading test), whether the mentoring meets the TCED-016 Beginning Teacher Support Program requirement, and whether the three years count as licensed teaching experience.

claims.text: A residency license may be converted to an Initial Professional License or a Continuing Professional License only if the applicant meets the IPL requirements in LICN-020 or the CPL requirements in LICN-024, and is recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

If the applicant meets these requirements by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL is effective on the date the requirements are met.

To qualify for a CPL as a teacher, an applicant must hold an IPL or residency license in North Carolina, satisfy the licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and have completed a Beginning Teacher Support Program under TCED-016 unless an exception applies.

The K-6 (Elementary, code 025) required tests are Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a required score of 233, and Pearson Test 203 Mathematics or Praxis Test 7813 CKT Math with a required score of 227 or 150. The table states that the Praxis code applies unless otherwise indicated, so a Praxis result alone does not show the Foundations of Reading requirement is met.
The CPL examination rule requires the exam to be taken at least once during the first year of licensure, if not already satisfied before the IPL, and passed before or during the third year.

The policies provided do not state whether the mentoring the teacher completed is the TCED-016 Beginning Teacher Support Program, and do not state whether years on a residency license count as licensed teaching experience under LICN-024 §1(c).

A CPL requires an EPP recommendation and the completed requirements, so the outcome depends on whether the teacher has an EPP recommendation, which target license (IPL or CPL) is intended, and whether the residency license's third year ends by June 30.

questions_for_user: Which Praxis or Pearson tests did the teacher pass, and what scores? Specifically, did they pass Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading (233) and the math requirement (Pearson 203 or Praxis 7813 at 227/150)?
Is the mentoring the Beginning Teacher Support Program under TCED-016, and was it completed?
Are the three years of teaching completed while holding the residency license, and are they licensed teaching years in North Carolina?
Is the teacher seeking conversion to an Initial Professional License or a Continuing Professional License?
Is the EPP that prepared the teacher recommending the conversion?
In which year of the residency license is the teacher, and will the requirements be met by June 30 of the third year?
premise_corrections: The question says the teacher 'passed Praxis.' For K-6 elementary, the table lists Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading as the required reading test, so passing Praxis may not satisfy the requirement.
not_covered: The IPL requirements in LICN-020, which apply if the teacher converts to an IPL.
The content of TCED-016 (Beginning Teacher Support Program), so it cannot be confirmed whether the mentoring completed qualifies.
Whether years on a residency license count as licensed teaching experience under LICN-024 §1(c).
Any fee for converting a residency license; LICN-008 does not list a residency conversion fee.
Whether the teacher's 'Praxis' results match the required scores, since the test score table is partly garbled in the passages.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the same needs_more_info verdict as the key, correctly states the EPP recommendation, CPL requirements, June 30 timing rule, and K-6 test requirements, and flags the Praxis-versus-Pearson issue and the unverifiable TCED-016 mentoring. It only partly addresses the exemptions and omits the one-year, twice-renewable residency term, both peripheral to the bottom line.

question: Teacher wants to be a school psychologist. Has an MA in school psych from Georgia, passed the NCSP exam, no NC license. Eligibility?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

input.query: Teacher wants to be a school psychologist. Has an MA in school psych from Georgia, passed the NCSP exam, no NC license. Eligibility?
NCSP nationally certified school psychologist continuing license out-of-state school psychologist
school psychologist specialist degree master's level eligibility out-of-state educator preparation program

answer.summary: The passages do not give a clear yes or no yet. If the educator holds a current NCSP credential, LICN-012 §6 says it entitles the holder to a continuing professional license, but the file must still show the degree level, any out-of-state license, and the required test or credential status before eligibility can be confirmed.

claims.text: School psychology is a student services personnel license area, and the student services personnel license is a 5-year renewable license issued to an individual who meets LICN-012.

A school psychologist license requires preparation at the advanced/specialist or doctoral degree level, and the NCSP credential issued by the National Association of School Psychologists entitles its holder to a continuing professional license.

Student services personnel licenses generally require completion of an EPP at the master's (M), specialist (S), or doctoral (D) level, and the license is issued at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP.

The passages do not define 'advanced' in 'advanced/specialist,' so they do not state whether a master's-level degree in school psychology alone satisfies LICN-012 §6. The analyst should confirm this against the full policy text.

The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the state where the EPP has its principal place of business. The passages do not say whether the Georgia program is recognized.

The NC testing table lists School Psychologist (code 026) with required Praxis test 5403 and required score 155. The passages do not list the NCSP credential or an NCSP exam as a substitute for that test.

Under LICN-012 §9, an applicant who satisfies the exam requirements before applying receives a continuing professional license, while one who does not but otherwise qualifies receives an initial professional license. The exam must be attempted in the first year and satisfied by the third year.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license by holding a license in the corresponding area in another jurisdiction, or by completing an EPP recognized by the jurisdiction where that EPP is based.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed experience may qualify for a continuing professional license only if they hold a clear out-of-state license, or hold NBPTS certification or substantially similar licensure requirements. Substantially similar requires an EPP recognized in its state and a passing out-of-state exam for each license area.
Out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial licensure in NC, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.
An applicant who completed an EPP based outside North Carolina may qualify for an initial professional license.
A complete application requires submitted documentation under LICN-004, the fee under LICN-008, and clearance from any SPI investigation if applicable.

questions_for_user: Does the educator hold a current, valid NCSP credential from NASP? Please provide the credential status and date.
Did the educator pass the Praxis School Psychologist test (5403) with a score of at least 155, or was the 'NCSP exam' a different test?
What is the highest degree level and the name and location of the school psychology program? Is the MA from an EPP recognized by Georgia or the SBE?
Does the educator hold any current Georgia (or other state) professional educator license, and if so, is it clear and in good standing?
How many years of licensed professional educator experience does the educator have, and in which jurisdictions?

question: What's the difference between an IPL and a CPL in NC?

input.query: What's the difference between an IPL and a CPL in NC?

answer.summary: An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license, while a CPL is a five-year, renewable license. Both let the holder practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina, but they differ in how they are earned, how they are renewed, and what happens when a CPL reverts to an IPL.

claims.text: An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license issued to an applicant or professional educator who meets SBE requirements.
A CPL is a five-year, renewable license issued to an applicant or professional educator who meets SBE requirements.
Both an IPL and a CPL entitle the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

To qualify for an IPL, an NC-prepared applicant must have completed a recognized NC educator preparation program and be recommended by the EPP. Other routes include an EPP based outside NC or a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

To qualify for a CPL as a teacher, an applicant must hold an IPL or residency license in NC, have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, satisfy the applicable licensure exam requirements, and complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.
A CPL remains in effect for five years after the licensee retires from full-time employment as a professional educator.

To renew a CPL, a teacher employed by a local board must have evidence of a rating of at least Proficient on the most recent annual evaluation, meaning Proficient or higher on three of the five Professional Teaching Standards, including Standard 4.

If a teacher with a current CPL in the final year of a renewal cycle is not deemed proficient, the LSAU may place the teacher on a mandatory improvement plan. If the teacher otherwise meets requirements, DPI issues an IPL, which lasts three years. At the end of that term the teacher may apply for a CPL if they meet the requirements, including required CEUs.
Reversion of a teacher's license from a CPL to an IPL is not a demotion in rank and does not reduce salary.

not_covered: The passages do not describe the salary or pay-scale differences between an IPL and a CPL beyond the reversion provision.
The passages do not specify the CEU requirements for renewal.
The passages do not give the full details of the Beginning Teacher Support Program.

incorrect_statements: The passages do not specify the CEU requirements for renewal.
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer gets the core difference right (three-year nonrenewable IPL versus five-year renewable CPL), the shared practice right, and the conversion and reversion rules, with every claim backed by its cited text. It omits the out-of-state exam restriction, the PSU route, the eight-CEU renewal details, and the administrator and student services CPL requirements, and wrongly says the CEU requirements are not in the passages.

question: What's the difference between a Residency License and an Initial Professional License?

input.query: What's the difference between a Residency License and an Initial Professional License?

answer.summary: A residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, requested by a school unit for an applicant who has either 24 hours of coursework or a passed licensure exam in the content area, and it carries ongoing enrollment, employment, and professional development requirements. An initial professional license (IPL) is a three-year nonrenewable license for applicants who completed an EPP or hold an out-of-state license with fewer than three years of experience, and it entitles the holder to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina. A residency license can convert to an IPL or CPL if the holder meets the IPL requirements and is recommended by the EPP by June 30 of the third year.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.
An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license issued to an applicant or professional educator who meets the relevant requirements established by SBE policy.

A residency license may be requested by the governing body of a public school unit (or an eligible nonpublic school) for an applicant under its employment who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination requirements.

To qualify for an IPL, an applicant must either have completed a recognized NC educator preparation program (EPP) and be recommended by it, have completed an EPP based outside North Carolina, or hold a clear out-of-state license and have fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

A school unit may request an IPL for an applicant who has completed all NC EPP requirements but has not yet satisfied the licensure examination requirements, and in that case the EPP recommendation is not required.
An IPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

To keep a residency license, the employing school unit must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program, is employed as a teacher in the unit, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license.

If a residency license holder fails to renew for the second or third year, the residency license expires, though the employing unit may request reinstatement if it hired the applicant within three years of the initial residency license's effective date and the license has not already been renewed twice.

To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 (or the CPL requirements in LICN-024) and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

If the applicant satisfies the conversion requirements by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL is effective when the requirements are later met.
A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for a permit to teach or an emergency license in the same license area.

A public school unit employing a residency license teacher must provide at least three hours of field experience before classroom teaching and at least 10 hours over the first year, plus 10 days of professional development covering listed topics, which may be done in the preservice period or split between preservice (five days) and the first year.

not_covered: Whether an IPL holder has any professional development or renewal requirements, since the passages provided do not address IPL renewal (an IPL is nonrenewable per the definition).
The full text of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which the residency eligibility rule incorporates by reference.
Whether residency license holders have the same practice rights as IPL holders, since LICN-020 §3 addresses only the IPL.
The CPL requirements referenced in LICN-024, which are not among the passages provided.
Any rules in effect before the 2026-07-01 effective date of these policies.

Every claim is backed by the cited LICN text. It omits peripheral points about the LICN-013 add-on restriction and that an IPL or residency holder can earn a CPL, but nothing it states is materially wrong.

question: Can you list the license types NCDPI issues to classroom teachers?

input.query: Can you list the license types NCDPI issues to classroom teachers?

answer.summary: The LICN-010 policy classifies teacher licenses into nine types: Initial Professional, Continuing Professional, Residency, Limited, Permit to Teach, Emergency, International Faculty, Lifetime, and Provisional. Each teacher is assigned one type based on qualifications. The passages name these types but do not explain the requirements for each one.

claims.text: Each teacher license is classified as one of the following based on the applicant's qualifications: Initial Professional License, Continuing Professional License, Residency License, Limited License, Permit to Teach, Emergency License, International Faculty License, Lifetime License, and Provisional License.
The Initial Professional License is provided under LICN-020.
The Continuing Professional License is provided under LICN-024.
The Residency License is provided under LICN-019, which defines it as a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.

The Limited License is provided under LICN-023, which defines it as a three-year renewable license issued to an individual who has completed an EPP but has not satisfied the applicable licensure examination requirements.
The Permit to Teach is provided under LICN-017.
The Emergency License is provided under LICN-018, which defines it as a one-year nonrenewable license.
The International Faculty License is provided under LICN-026.
The Lifetime License is provided under LICN-027, which defines it as a license requiring no renewal.
The Provisional License is provided under LICN-014. LICN-001 separately defines a Provisional assistant principal license, which is a different license type.

At the top level, DPI issues three license classifications: Teacher, Administrator, and Student Services Personnel. The Teacher classification covers an individual whose major responsibility is to teach or directly supervise teaching.

question: Is there still a Permit to Teach in NC, and who is it for?

input.query: Is there still a Permit to Teach in NC, and who is it for?

answer.summary: The current LICN policies still provide a Permit to Teach. A public school unit may request one for an applicant it employs who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license. Validity: a permit to teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested, and it cannot be extended or renewed.

Pay: for State Salary Schedule certification, a permit to teach is issued at the level of a bachelor's degree (A-Level) teacher license with zero years of experience, regardless of the applicant's education level or prior work experience.
Add-on areas: the DPI may not add additional teaching license areas to a Permit to Teach.
